source_evidence.anchor: equation (1.1) and the one-dimensional RMS convention
source_evidence.observation: The paper defines the complex, unnormalized Fourier transform with kernel exp(i 2 pi jk/N), zero-based indices, and RMS norm equal to the square root of the mean squared complex modulus.

source_evidence.anchor: equation (2.2) and the FFT matrix factorization
source_evidence.observation: The one-dimensional FFT is represented by permutation, block-Fourier, and diagonal twiddle-factor matrices. The factorization applies to Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey variants, with different diagonal matrices.
Floating-point addition and multiplication are modeled deterministically using a computer-dependent epsilon and generic factors theta with absolute value at most one.
Computed sine and cosine values satisfy an absolute error model with gamma greater than or equal to zero; gamma depends on transform order and implementation but is independent of input data.

source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 1 and the definition of K(N,gamma)
source_evidence.observation: For a chosen mixed-radix factorization, Theorem 1 defines K as the sum of per-radix alpha constants plus one 3+2 gamma contribution for each interstage diagonal multiplication.
The proof expands the floating-point factors and places terms of order epsilon squared into O(epsilon^2).
The exact multidimensional transform is indexed by m coordinate pairs, with s_l and t_l ranging from zero through N_l minus one.
The paper defines pointwise output error, multidimensional RMS error, and maximum error. Theorem 2(a) gives the selected relative RMS bound; Theorem 2(b) gives a separate maximum-error companion.

source_evidence.anchor: nested computation, telescoping decomposition, and equations (4.2)-(4.4)
source_evidence.observation: The proof writes the transform as successive coordinate transforms, decomposes total error into propagated local errors, bounds each local error using Theorem 1, and uses exact RMS scaling by sqrt(N_l).

source_evidence.anchor: completion of the proof of Theorem 2(a) and Section 6 exact-input statement
source_evidence.observation: The local scaling factors cancel to produce the sum of coordinatewise K constants. The proof requires the input RMS to be exact or correct through first order, and Section 6 states that the preceding analysis assumed exactly representable input data.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 6 continuation using a fictional input perturbation
source_evidence.observation: The paper gives a one-dimensional backward interpretation of output roundoff as an exact Fourier transform of a fictional input perturbation; it does not state a multidimensional input-rounding extension of Theorem 2(a).

binders: Let m be the number of transform dimensions and let N_l be the length of coordinate l for l=1,...,m; the displayed index convention is s_l,t_l=0,1,...,N_l-1. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1).]

Let X(s_1,...,s_m) be complex input data and Y(t_1,...,t_m) its exact multidimensional Fourier transform. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1).]

Let epsilon be the computer-dependent arithmetic error constant, let each occurrence of theta lie in [-1,1], and let gamma be the nonnegative absolute sine/cosine error constant. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model.]

For each coordinate l, K(N_l,gamma) is instantiated from the mixed-radix factorization used by that coordinate's one-dimensional FFT. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,gamma); PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
hypotheses: The exact output satisfies Y(t_1,...,t_m)=sum_{s_1}...sum_{s_m} e(s_1 t_1/N_1+...+s_m t_m/N_m)X(s_1,...,s_m), with every sum taken over the corresponding zero-based coordinate range. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1).]

The computed output fl(Y) is obtained by a multidimensional fast Fourier transform implemented as successive one-dimensional FFTs along the coordinates. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: nested computation fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)).]

Each coordinate FFT is covered by the floating-point mixed-radix analysis of Theorem 1, including separate diagonal twiddle-factor multiplications. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and the parenthetical following K(N,gamma).]

Arithmetic and trigonometric evaluations obey equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the absolute sine/cosine error model. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model.]

Exact representability of the input data is inherited from the paper's standing scope, although it is not repeated in the displayed statement of Theorem 2(a); the proof says first-order preservation of the input RMS is sufficient for its final step. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a) and Section 6 exact-input statement.]
conclusions: The selected conclusion is [fl(Y)-Y]_RMS/Y_RMS <= epsilon sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
definitions_and_conventions: E(t_1,...,t_m)=fl(Y(t_1,...,t_m))-Y(t_1,...,t_m). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional error definition.]
[fl(Y)-Y]_RMS is the square root of sum_{t_1}...sum_{t_m}|E(t_1,...,t_m)|^2 divided by N_1...N_m. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional RMS definition.]

Y_RMS denotes the corresponding RMS value of the exact output Y; this use follows the paper's RMS convention, although Section 4 does not separately display its formula. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a) denominator; PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: RMS convention.]

If a coordinate length N_l is factored as N_l=product_{j=1}^{M_l} r_{l,j}, then K(N_l,gamma)=sum_{j=1}^{M_l} alpha(r_{l,j})+(M_l-1)(3+2 gamma). This relabels Theorem 1's radix factors to avoid collision with the multidimensional coordinate index. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,gamma).]
The per-radix constant is alpha(r)=sqrt(2) for r=2, alpha(r)=5 for r=4, and alpha(r)=2 sqrt(r)(r+gamma) otherwise. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: definition of alpha(N_l).]

Equation (4.1) literally writes the kernel as e(q); comparison with equations (1.1) and (2.1) indicates the intended positive-sign complex exponential exp(i 2 pi q), but that shorthand is not explicitly defined in Section 4. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1).]
implicit_context: The transform is complex and unnormalized: the one-dimensional convention uses exp(i 2 pi jk/N), with i=sqrt(-1), and contains no forward factor 1/N. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1).]

The same displayed Theorem 2 has a companion clause (b): [fl(Y)-Y]_MAX/Y_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_1...N_m) sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2). It is the maximum-error clause, distinct from selected clause (a). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(b).]
The inherited one-dimensional factorization covers Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey forms, with different diagonal matrices D_j. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: remarks following equation (2.2).]

The proof is deterministic and accumulates worst-case local error bounds additively; it invokes no independence or statistical roundoff assumption. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: telescoping decomposition and equation (4.2).]
statement.algorithm_linkage: Define Z_0=Y and Z_m=X, and for l=1,...,m define Z_{l-1}=T_l Z_l by Z_{l-1}(s_1,...,s_{l-1},t_l,...,t_m)=sum_{s_l} e(s_l t_l/N_l)Z_l(s_1,...,s_l,t_{l+1},...,t_m). The computed nesting is fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)). Its exact telescoping decomposition propagates each local term fl(T_l fl(Z_l))-T_l fl(Z_l) through T_1...T_{l-1}. Equation (4.3) gives [fl(Z_{l-1})-Z_{l-1}]_RMS/[Z_l]_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_l)K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2), while equation (4.4) gives [Z_{l-1}]_RMS=sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS. Iterating the scaling makes every propagated first-order term proportional to Y_RMS and yields the sum over l in Theorem 2(a). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: nested computation, telescoping decomposition, and equations (4.2)-(4.4); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a).]
numerical_model: For floating-point numbers a and b, fl(a+b)=a(1+theta epsilon)+b(1+theta epsilon) and fl(ab)=ab(1+theta epsilon), where theta is generic, usually differs at each occurrence, and always lies in [-1,1]. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2).]

With at least t+1 digits used to accumulate sums, epsilon=0.5 beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and epsilon=beta^(1-t) for chopped operations, where beta is the base and t is the mantissa length. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchor: paragraph following equation (3.2).]

If sums are accumulated with only t digits, epsilon=0.5(1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and epsilon=(1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for chopped operations. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: continuation of the paragraph following equation (3.2).]

Trigonometric computation obeys fl(sin(fl(a)))=sin(a)+gamma theta epsilon and fl(cos(fl(a)))=cos(a)+gamma theta epsilon. This is an absolute-error model, not a relative-error model. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model.]

Gamma is nonnegative, depends on how the trigonometric functions and their arguments are computed for a given transform order, and is independent of the input data. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: paragraph following the sine/cosine model.]
error_notions: The selected numerator is forward output error: the RMS of computed values minus exact Fourier-transform values. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: definition of E and multidimensional RMS error.]

The selected relative measure divides global RMS output error by the global RMS value of the exact output; it is not a componentwise relative error and does not divide by the computed output. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
The final first-order coefficient is an additive sum over coordinate FFTs, not a root-sum-square statistical combination. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.2) and Theorem 2(a).]

Input-representation error is outside the selected bound; the paper says a further term is required when the input is not exactly representable. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: Section 6 exact-input statement.]
norms: All multidimensional RMS quantities average squared complex moduli over all N_1...N_m entries. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional RMS definition.]
For each exact coordinate transform, [Z_{l-1}]_RMS=sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.4).]

Consequently, [Z_l]_RMS=sqrt(N_{l+1}...N_m)[X]_RMS and Y_RMS=sqrt(N_1...N_m)X_RMS under the unnormalized transform. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: propagated scaling in the completion of Theorem 2(a).]

The selected denominator is the exact output RMS, so a nonzero denominator is mathematically required even though the theorem does not state that side condition. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
constants_and_indexing: Coordinate indices are zero-based, while the dimension index l runs from 1 through m. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: index convention following equation (4.1).]

For each coordinate, the radix-factor index runs through its chosen factorization and contributes one alpha value per radix plus M_l-1 copies of 3+2 gamma. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: K(N,gamma).]

For radix-2 and radix-4 one-dimensional algorithms, Theorem 1 specializes the constant to K(2^M,gamma)=(3+sqrt(2)+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma) and K(4^M,gamma)=(8+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: radix-2 and radix-4 specializations.]
The K constants include separate multiplications by D_j for j=1,...,M-1. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: parenthetical following the radix specializations.]

The selected multidimensional coefficient is exactly sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma); no factor sqrt(N_1...N_m) remains in clause (a). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of its proof.]
higher_order_terms: The selected result retains an additive O(epsilon^2) term after the first-order coefficient epsilon sum_l K(N_l,gamma). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]

The derivation groups terms of order epsilon squared into O(epsilon^2), and uses [fl(Z_l)]_RMS=[Z_l]_RMS+O(epsilon) when replacing computed intermediate norms. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: first-order expansion; PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a).]

The paper does not specify the hidden O(epsilon^2) constant, its uniformity, an explicit epsilon range, or its dependence on dimensions, factorization, gamma, and data. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a); PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: description of O(epsilon^2).]
exceptional_values: The ratio in Theorem 2(a) is undefined when Y_RMS=0, and the displayed theorem supplies no nonzero-output hypothesis or zero-output convention. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]

The arithmetic model discusses bounded relative perturbations and trigonometric absolute errors but states no treatment of overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, NaNs, or other exceptional machine values. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the sine/cosine model.]

Nonexact input data requires an additional input-rounding contribution; no multidimensional version of that contribution is included in Theorem 2(a). [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: Section 6 exact-input statement and additional-term discussion.]

undebatable_constraints: The selected claim is the relative RMS inequality [fl(Y)-Y]_RMS/Y_RMS <= epsilon sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]

The exact transform is a complex product-indexed multidimensional Fourier transform with zero-based coordinate indices and no forward normalization factor. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1).]
The numerator is a global RMS forward error and the denominator is the RMS of the exact output. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: multidimensional RMS definition and Theorem 2(a).]
Every dimension contributes its own full Theorem 1 constant K(N_l,gamma), and these constants are added over l=1,...,m. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]

K is factorization-sensitive and includes alpha(r)=sqrt(2) for radix 2, alpha(r)=5 for radix 4, alpha(r)=2 sqrt(r)(r+gamma) otherwise, plus (M-1)(3+2 gamma). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,gamma).]

The proof uses the exact local scaling [Z_{l-1}]_RMS=sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS, which cancels the local sqrt(N_l) factors in the final relative bound. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: equations (4.3)-(4.4); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a).]

The result is a first-order deterministic floating-point bound using the stated addition, multiplication, and absolute trigonometric error models, with all remaining terms represented by O(epsilon^2). [PDF pp. 2-4, printed pp. 758-760, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2), sine/cosine model, and first-order expansion.]

The preceding analysis assumes input data exactly representable in machine precision, although this scope is stated after Theorem 2 rather than in its displayed hypotheses. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: Section 6 exact-input statement.]

ambiguities.issue: Equation (4.1) uses e(q) without explicitly defining that notation in Section 4. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1).]
ambiguities.evidence: The one-dimensional transform and matrix entries use exp(i 2 pi q), while the multidimensional equation switches to e(q) without a displayed definition. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1); PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1).]
ambiguities.impact: Identifying e(q) with exp(i 2 pi q) is strongly indicated but inherited or inferred rather than locally explicit; a formal statement should record that interpretation instead of silently treating it as a new arbitrary function. [PDF pp. 1, 2, and 7, anchors: equations (1.1), (2.1), and (4.1).]

ambiguities.issue: Section 4 uses Y_RMS in the theorem denominator without separately displaying its multidimensional formula. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.evidence: The page explicitly defines the RMS of fl(Y)-Y, while the general RMS convention appears earlier for vectors. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional RMS definition; PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: RMS convention.]
ambiguities.impact: The natural contract applies the same product-indexed RMS formula to exact Y, but this is an inherited convention rather than a new explicit definition on the theorem page. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: multidimensional RMS definition and Theorem 2(a).]

ambiguities.issue: The notation K(N,gamma) suppresses dependence on the chosen mixed-radix factorization and hence on the concrete one-dimensional FFT variant. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,gamma).]
ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 1 first assumes N=N_1...N_M and then defines K by summing alpha over those factors, with separate diagonal-multiplication contributions. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and the parenthetical following K.]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization cannot determine K from the integer N alone unless it also fixes a factorization or chooses a bound over factorizations. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: K(N,gamma).]

ambiguities.issue: Theorem 2 uses one gamma for all coordinate lengths even though gamma is said to depend on transformation order and implementation. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: sine/cosine model; PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 2 writes sum_l K(N_l,gamma) with a single gamma, but the earlier definition describes gamma as order-dependent. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: paragraph following the sine/cosine model; PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.impact: The paper does not say whether gamma is identical for every coordinate FFT or is a common upper bound for coordinate-specific constants; replacing it by gamma_l would be an interpretation, not the literal statement. [PDF pp. 3 and 8, anchors: sine/cosine model and Theorem 2(a).]

ambiguities.issue: Exact input representability is not written in Theorem 2(a)'s displayed hypotheses. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.evidence: The proof closes by assuming the input RMS is exact or differs only by O(epsilon), and Section 6 later states that the preceding analysis assumed exactly representable input data. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchors: completion of Theorem 2(a) and Section 6 exact-input statement.]
ambiguities.impact: Exact input is inherited scope. For nonexact input, an additional contribution is required, but the paper does not state its multidimensional form in Theorem 2(a). [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: input-rounding discussion.]

ambiguities.issue: The meaning and uniformity of O(epsilon^2) are not quantified. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.evidence: The proof only says that O(epsilon^2) includes terms of order epsilon squared and supplies no hidden constant or admissible epsilon interval. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: first-order expansion.]
ambiguities.impact: The displayed result is a first-order asymptotic error statement, not a fully explicit finite-epsilon inequality unless additional bounds on the omitted terms are supplied. [PDF pp. 4 and 8, anchors: first-order expansion and Theorem 2(a).]

ambiguities.issue: The theorem does not exclude Y_RMS=0 even though it divides by Y_RMS. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.evidence: No nonzero-output or nonzero-input side condition accompanies the displayed ratio. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]
ambiguities.impact: A literal formal ratio theorem needs a nonzero-denominator hypothesis or an explicit convention for the zero transform. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a).]

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point values and range failures are outside the stated model. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the sine/cosine model.]
ambiguities.evidence: The model specifies bounded perturbations for ordinary arithmetic and trigonometric results but gives no overflow, underflow, subnormal, infinity, or NaN conditions. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the sine/cosine model.]
ambiguities.impact: Any formal theorem using this contract must either assume all operations remain within the ordinary modeled range or add exceptional-value semantics not present in the paper. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the sine/cosine model.]

contract_plain_english: For an m-dimensional complex, unnormalized Fourier transform with coordinate lengths N_1,...,N_m, compute the output by applying one-dimensional mixed-radix FFTs successively along the coordinates. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: nested computation.] Under the paper's deterministic floating-point and absolute trigonometric error models, and within its inherited exact-input scope, Theorem 2(a) says that the global RMS output error divided by the exact output RMS is at most epsilon times the sum of the one-dimensional constants K(N_l,gamma), plus terms of order epsilon squared. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and sine/cosine model; PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: exact-input statement.] Each K is determined by the actual radix factorization used for that coordinate, including the special radix-2 and radix-4 constants and interstage twiddle multiplications. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,gamma).] The proof adds propagated local RMS bounds and uses exact sqrt(N_l) norm scaling so those dimensional factors cancel from the final relative-RMS coefficient. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: equations (4.2)-(4.4); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a).]
